introduction: These readings start from one observation, that nothing in existence is at rest, and follow it in several directions. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá distinguishes kinds of motion, of place, of growth, of quality and of spirit; says that motion is the sign of life and stagnation of death; describes the atoms in perpetual travel and every system as turning about a centre; and applies the rule to people, who must advance or fall back. Bahá’u’lláh adds that heat is the cause of motion, and that the heat meant is the love of God. All seventy-four quotations are read here beside seventy-four from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: Heraclitus's river and fire, Ecclesiastes on the circuits of sun and wind, Plato's moving image of eternity, Aristotle's mover that moves by being loved, Dante's love that moves the sun, Wordsworth, Coleridge, Darwin, Tennyson's Ulysses. Eight push back or add a side: the psalm that says the earth cannot be moved, Malachi's unchanging God, Khayyam's moving finger, Pascal on the man who cannot sit still, 'be still, and know', Isaiah's strength in quietness, and the Preacher, for whom all this motion brings nothing new.
questions: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá lists motions of place, growth, quality and spirit. Give an example of each from your own life.
'Absolute repose does not exist in nature.' What, then, do Malachi's 'I change not' and the psalm's 'be still' refer to?
The readings say that whoever stops, descends. Pascal blames our unhappiness on being unable to stay quietly in a room. How do you tell progress from restlessness?
The Preacher sees endless motion and nothing new. What do the readings add that turns motion into progress?
Bahá’u’lláh calls heat the cause of motion and names the love of God. What sets a person moving, and what keeps them going?
Each system is said to turn about a centre. What is the centre of your own?

outside.why: Heraclitus said that upon those who step into the same rivers, different and ever different waters flow.
Shelley wrote that man's yesterday may never be like his morrow: nought may endure but mutability.
Newton, who described the clockwork of the heavens, said we know God only by his most wise and excellent contrivances of things.
Emerson saw the circle repeated without end through nature, the highest emblem in the cipher of the world.
Jesus describes growth at its own pace: first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear.
The Qur'an says of sun and moon, night and day: they float each in an orbit.
Ecclesiastes watches the sun arise and go down, and the wind whirl about continually and return on its circuits.
A psalm pictures the sun as a strong man rejoicing to run a race from one end of heaven to the other.
Paul speaks of a change that ascends: we are changed into the same image from glory to glory.
Heraclitus said the way up and the way down are one and the same. Can ascent and descent be told apart while they are happening?
Ecclesiastes says that to every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.
Aristotle held that the elements are by nature such as to change into one another, coming to be out of contraries.
Marcus Aurelius asks us to observe how all things in the universe act with one movement.
Plato says the maker set the heavens in order as a moving image of eternity, moving according to number.
A psalm sings that the world is stablished, that it cannot be moved. What happened when such lines were read as a statement about the earth and the sun?
Wordsworth felt a motion and a spirit that impels all thinking things and rolls through all things.
Paul told the Athenians, quoting their own poets, that in God we live, and move, and have our being.
Coleridge sensed one life within us and abroad, which meets all motion and becomes its soul.
Darwin found grandeur in the view that from so simple a beginning endless forms have been, and are being, evolved.
Shakespeare watched the waves make towards the shore, each changing place with that which goes before.
Jesus compares the Spirit to the wind, which bloweth where it listeth, and none can tell whence it comes.
Tennyson's Ulysses finds it dull to pause, to make an end, to rust unburnished, not to shine in use.
Ariel sings of a change of kind: nothing of him that doth fade, but doth suffer a sea-change into something rich and strange.
Plato's Timaeus notes how water, by condensing, becomes stone and earth, and by dispersing, vapour and air.
Marcus Aurelius says that death is such as generation is, a mystery of nature.
Heraclitus called the world an ever-living fire, kindled in measures and going out in measures.
The Buddha taught that decay is inherent in all component things, and told his followers to work diligently.
Shelley addresses the west wind as a wild spirit moving everywhere, destroyer and preserver.
Lucretius built his poem of moving atoms on the rule that nothing from nothing ever yet was born.
Leibniz held that each simple substance expresses all the others, a perpetual living mirror of the universe.
Blake would see a world in a grain of sand, and hold infinity in the palm of the hand.
Dante begins his Paradise with the glory of him who moveth everything, shining through the universe.
The Tao Te Ching says the Tao produced One, One produced Two, Two produced Three, and Three produced all things.
Descartes held that conserving a substance from moment to moment needs the same power as creating it.
Aristotle's own account is that the final cause produces motion as being loved, and all other things move by being moved.
For Aristotle the first mover's activity is thought, and its thinking is a thinking on thinking.
A psalm says the heavens shall wax old like a garment and be changed, but God endures.
Malachi hears God say: I am the Lord, I change not. If motion belongs to everything that exists, what is it that does not move?
Paul says that we have many members in one body, and all members have not the same office.
Paul adds that if one member suffer, all the members suffer with it.
Ephesians pictures a body fitly joined together, every joint supplying its measure.
Jesus says: I am the vine, ye are the branches; without me ye can do nothing.
Plato likens the good to the sun, which gives visible things both their being seen and their growth.
Malachi promises that the Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in his wings.
Plotinus compares what proceeds from the One to the brilliant light encircling the sun, ceaselessly generated from it.
Augustine addresses a God most hidden and most near, and piles up the opposites that meet in him.
Jesus said that not one sparrow shall fall on the ground without your Father.
Jeremiah found the word in his heart as a burning fire shut up in his bones, and he could not stay.
A psalmist says: my heart was hot within me; while I was musing the fire burned; then spake I with my tongue.
The Song of Songs says the coals of love are coals of fire, which many waters cannot quench.
Isaiah says that they that wait upon the Lord shall mount up with wings as eagles.
John Wesley wrote in his journal of the evening he felt his heart strangely warmed.
Shakespeare's Cassius says the fault is not in our stars, but in ourselves, that we are underlings.
Proverbs says that a man's heart deviseth his way, but the Lord directeth his steps.
Khayyam says the moving finger writes and moves on, and no piety or wit can cancel half a line. If one power moves all things, what is left to human action?
Rumi tells the same progress as his own: I died as mineral and became a plant, I died as plant and rose to animal.
Whitman says his feet strike an apex of the apices of the stairs, on every step bunches of ages.
In the parable the owner seeks fruit on his fig tree three years and finds none, and the dresser asks one year more.
Pascal traced all the unhappiness of men to their not being able to stay quietly in their own chamber. Is weariness of one place a law of nature, or a weakness?
The Qur'an tells people to travel in the land and see the consequence for those who were before.
Abraham's story begins with a command to move: get thee out of thy country, unto a land that I will shew thee.
Paul says: forgetting those things which are behind, I press toward the mark.
Tennyson's old sailors are resolved to strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.
A psalm says: be still, and know that I am God. Is every pause the beginning of a fall?
Proverbs says the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day.
Jesus said that no man who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom.
Longfellow would have us act so that each tomorrow finds us farther than today.
Tennyson cried: forward, forward let us range; let the great world spin for ever down the ringing grooves of change.
The Preacher sees motion without progress: what has been is what shall be, and there is no new thing under the sun. Are movement and progress the same law?
Isaiah says: in returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength. What place has stillness in a world that never rests?
Job says: these are parts of his ways, but how little a portion is heard of him.
Plato speaks of a divinity that moves people as the magnet stone attracts iron rings and gives them its own power.
Dante ends with his desire and will turning like a wheel, moved by the Love which moves the sun and the other stars.
Augustine says to God: our hearts are restless until they rest in you.
